TRANSCRIBER'S NOTE:


Italic text has been marked with _underscores_. In the book the Latin
text is printed on the left page, and the English translation on the
right. Here, the text is split by sections starting with a roman
numeral, and the Latin text is followed by its English translation.
Sidenotes are placed between #hashtags#.




INTRODUCTION


In the _de Officiis_ we have, save for the latter Philippics, the great
orator's last contribution to literature.




BOOK I

MORAL GOODNESS




LIBER PRIMUS / BOOK I


*1* I. Quamquam te, Marce fili, annum iam audientem Cratippum, idque
Athenis, abundare oportet praeceptis institutisque philosophiae et
ad dicendum[1] et ad iudicandum.

*2* Quam ob rem disces tu quidem a principe huius aetatis philosophorum,
et disces, quam diu voles.

    [1] _dicendum_ Edd.; _discendum_ MSS. (i.e. acquisition of
    learning).


#Introduction: the importance of combining Greek and Latin studies.#

*1* I. My dear son Marcus, you have now been studying a full year under
Cratippus, and that too in Athens, and you should be fully equipped
with the practical precepts and the principles of philosophy.

#Greek Philosophy and Cicero's own.#

*2* You will, therefore, learn from the foremost of present-day
philosophers, and you will go on learning as long as you wish; and
these[A] books of mine on philosophy.

    [A] Cicero's technical terms are difficult because he has to
    invent them to translate Greek that is perfectly simple:

    _rectum_ is 'right,' i.e. perfect, absolute. Its opposite is
    _medium_, 'mean,' i.e. intermediate.


II. Sed cum statuissem scribere ad te aliquid hoc tempore, multa
posthac, ab eo ordiri maxime volui, quod et aetati tuae esset aptissimum
et auctoritati meae.

L. Minuci Basili, locupletis hominis, falsum testamentum quidam e
Graecia Romam attulerunt.

#de Fin. II, 12 ff.; Tusc. Disp. IV-V; de Off. III, 117#

              Núlla sancta sócietas
    Néc fides regni ést,

#Statement of subject.#

II. But since I have decided to write you a little now (and a great deal
by and by), I wish, if possible, to begin with a matter most suited at
once to your years and to my position.

    "There is no fellowship inviolate,
    No faith is kept, when kingship is concerned;"




BOOK II

EXPEDIENCY




LIBER SECUNDUS / BOOK II


*1* I. Quem ad modum officia ducerentur ab honestate, Marce fili, satis
explicatum arbitror libro superiore.

*1* I. I believe, Marcus, my son, that I have fully explained in the
preceding book how duties are derived from moral rectitude.

*5* II. Maximis igitur in malis hoc tamen boni assecuti videmur. *7*
III. Quinque igitur rationibus propositis officii persequendi.

*5* II. Therefore, amid all the present most awful calamities I yet
flatter myself that I have won this good out of evil. *7* III. Five
principles, accordingly, have been laid down.

*9* IV. Tecta vero, quibus et frigorum vis pelleretur et calorum
molestiae sedarentur.

*9* IV. And how could houses ever have been provided in the first place
to keep off the severity of cold and alleviate the discomforts of heat?


*44* (IV.) Sed ut facillime, quales simus, tales esse videamur, etsi
in eo ipso vis maxima est, tamen quaedam praecepta danda sunt.


*44* (IV.) But although the very essence of the problem is that we
actually be what we wish to be thought to be, still some rules may be
laid down.




INDEX


References are to Book and Section; all dates, given in parentheses
(...), are B.C.

Academicians.
  1. adherents of the New Academy (_q.v._);
    their right to teach ethics, I, 6;
  2. adherents of the Old Academy, III, 20.
